Clocks on servers drift because the hardware that keeps time is never perfectly stable. Each system clock is driven by a quartz oscillator that ticks at a nominal frequency, but manufacturing tolerances, temperature changes, aging of the crystal, and voltage fluctuations all cause the tick rate to deviate slightly from exactly what it should be, so the clock gains or loses some number of milliseconds per day relative to true time. Virtualization adds another source of error, since a guest VM may not receive ticks while its host is descheduled, and the kernel's software counter can also skip or double up around suspend, hibernation, or NTP step corrections. Because uncorrected drift accumulates into seconds and then minutes of skew, servers rely on the Network Time Protocol or PTP daemons to continuously compare against authoritative time sources and nudge the clock back into alignment.
